protestant.communion:
Protestants call the meal the Lord's Supper, also the Lord's Table or Holy Communion. It was instituted by Christ on the night he was betrayed, using bread and the cup as he commanded: 'Do this in remembrance of me.' Churches differ on what is received. Some teach that Christ is truly present with the elements for believers; others treat the act as a memorial of his death and a pledge of belonging to him. Almost all agree it is not a repetition of Calvary.

It is ordinarily celebrated in gathered worship, after the Word is preached. Who may come, how often it is held, and whether wine or juice is used vary by church. The common conviction is that the Lord's Supper proclaims the Lord's death until he comes and binds the congregation to him and to one another.
protestant.trinity:
Protestants confess the Trinity: one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, equal in deity and glory. This is the God of the creeds received from the early church and of the Scriptures that name the Father, the Son, and the Spirit as God without dividing the divine being into three gods.

The triune God is the source of creation, redemption, and the church's life. Prayer is offered to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Disputes among Protestants rarely concern whether God is triune; they concern how the persons relate in salvation and in the church's speech about God.
protestant.father:
God the Father is the first person of the Trinity, the maker of heaven and earth, from whom the Son is eternally begotten and the Spirit proceeds. Protestants speak of him as Heavenly Father because Christ taught his disciples to pray 'Our Father' and because the gospel adopts believers as children of God.

The Father sent the Son and raised him from the dead. Worship is directed to him without treating the Son or the Spirit as lesser gods. Language about the Father's will, love, and holiness is drawn first from Scripture rather than from later speculation about inner-Trinitarian life.
protestant.holy_spirit:
The Holy Spirit, often also called the Holy Ghost in older Protestant speech, is the third person of the Trinity, fully God, not a mere force. He inspired the prophets and apostles, applies Christ's work to believers, gives new birth, and dwells in the church.

Protestants differ on whether certain sign gifts continue and on how the Spirit's filling is experienced, but they agree that no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Spirit, and that the Spirit's ordinary work is to glorify Christ and form holy lives through the Word.
protestant.filioque:
Most Protestants inherited the Western wording of the Nicene Creed and say the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Filioque. They take this to guard the full deity of the Son and the unity of the triune work of salvation: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

Some Protestant scholars and some Anglican and Lutheran conversations with the East treat the clause as a later Latin addition that need not divide the churches. The living issue for most Protestants is not the medieval controversy itself but whether their confession of the Spirit remains fully Trinitarian and biblical.
protestant.incarnation:
The Incarnation is the confession that the eternal Son became man: God became man in Jesus of Nazareth, born of Mary, without ceasing to be God. Protestants read John's prologue and the infancy narratives as history and as the center of the gospel. The Word made flesh lived, suffered, died, and rose in a real body.

This rules out treating Jesus as only a prophet or only an appearance of God. Churches may differ on later Marian titles, but they do not differ on the fact of the Incarnation as the ground of salvation.
protestant.natures_of_christ:
Protestants confess that Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures in one person, following the line of Chalcedon even when they do not recite that council by name. The one Lord Jesus is not a mixture that is less than God or less than man.

How the two natures relate in his suffering and knowledge is discussed with care. The pastoral point is constant: only one who is God can save, and only one who is truly man can stand in our place.
protestant.virgin_birth:
Protestants teach the virgin birth: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, as the Gospels of Matthew and Luke narrate. It marks him as the promised Son, not the product of ordinary human generation.

The doctrine is held as biblical history, not as a later decoration. It is not usually treated as the main proof of his deity, which rests on his person, works, death, and resurrection, but as part of the one story of the Incarnation.
protestant.preexistence_of_christ:
The Son is the eternal Son, the preexistent Christ, the Word who was with God and was God before Bethlehem. Protestants read the statements of John, Paul, and Hebrews as teaching that the person who became Jesus already was, not that a man was later raised to divine rank.

This confession separates historic Protestant faith from views that date the Son's beginning at his conception or treat him as the first created being. The child in the manger is the same Lord through whom all things were made.
protestant.atonement:
The atonement is Christ's saving death. Protestants commonly speak of penal substitution: he bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners, so that forgiveness is just as well as merciful. Other biblical images—victory over death, sacrifice, ransom, reconciliation—are also used, and churches weigh them differently.

The cross is finished work, not a ritual to be repeated. Faith receives what Christ accomplished there. Disputes about the extent of the atonement (for the elect, or sufficient for all) run through Reformed and other Protestant bodies, but the center remains the same: Christ died for sins according to the Scriptures.
protestant.resurrection_of_christ:
The resurrection of Jesus is bodily and historical. The tomb was empty, and the risen Lord appeared to his witnesses. Protestants treat this as the Father's public vindication of the Son and the firstfruits of the resurrection of the dead.

Without the empty tomb the preaching of the cross would be empty. Easter is therefore not a symbol of spring or of inner renewal only; it is the announcement that death did not hold him, and will not hold those who are his.
protestant.ascension:
The ascension of Christ is his going to the Father's right hand in the same risen body, there to reign, intercede, and send the Spirit. He is not absent in the sense of being idle; he is absent from earthly sight until he comes again.

From that place he is head of the church and will return. Protestant worship looks up to a living Lord, not only back to a remembered teacher.
protestant.offices_of_christ:
Many Protestants, especially in the Reformed family, speak of Christ as prophet, priest, and king, the threefold office. As prophet he reveals the Father and the gospel; as priest he offered himself and still intercedes; as king he rules the church and the world.

The scheme is a way of gathering Scripture, not a fourth creed. Churches that do not use the phrase still ascribe to him the same work under other words.
protestant.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Spiritual gifts are the Spirit's distributions for the common good of the church: teaching, service, leadership, mercy, and, in some congregations, gifts of healing, prophecy, and tongues. Protestants take 1 Corinthians 12–14 and similar texts as still describing the church's life, though they disagree about which gifts belong to the apostolic age only.

The test of a gift is whether it builds up the body and agrees with Scripture. Gifts are not a second gospel beside justification by faith.
protestant.tongues:
Tongues, sometimes called the gift of languages, appear in the New Testament as Spirit-given speech. Protestant opinion divides. Some hold that the gift was a sign for the apostolic foundation of the church and has ceased in that form. Others hold that it may still be given, to be used in order and with interpretation in public worship.

Few Protestant bodies treat tongues as the required sign of salvation. The shared concern is that worship remain intelligible and that no gift be used to create two classes of Christians.
protestant.justification:
Justification is God's declaring the sinner righteous through faith in Christ. Classic Protestant teaching speaks of imputed righteousness: Christ's obedience is counted to the believer, not infused as a quality that then earns acceptance. It is by grace, received by faith, not by works of the law.

Sanctification follows as the fruit, not the basis, of this verdict. Later Protestant theology has debated how closely justification and the new life should be described together, but the Reformation watchword remains: God justifies the ungodly who trust in Christ.
protestant.sanctification:
Sanctification is being made holy. The same grace that justifies also sets the believer apart and trains him or her in love of God and neighbor. It is the Spirit's work through the Word, prayer, the sacraments or ordinances, and the fellowship of the church.

Protestants reject both carelessness after conversion and any claim of sinless perfection that denies remaining sin. Holiness movements within Protestantism speak of a deeper work of grace; others speak of lifelong growth. Both intend obedience that answers justification.
protestant.glorification:
Glorification is the final redemption of the believer, when the dead in Christ are raised and the living are changed, free from sin and death. It completes what justification began and what sanctification has been working.

Hope is not escape from the body but the raising of the body. Protestant preaching of glory is meant to steady perseverance, not to feed speculation about ranks in heaven.
protestant.theosis:
When Protestants speak of union with Christ or, more rarely, deification, they mean sharing the life of the risen Lord by the Spirit, not becoming a fourth member of the Godhead. Believers are adopted, conformed to Christ's image, and will see him as he is.

The word theosis is not native Protestant vocabulary. The reality it names in other traditions is usually handled under union with Christ, adoption, and glorification, always under the Creator-creature distinction.
protestant.grace:
Grace is unmerited favor, God's kindly movement toward sinners who cannot save themselves. It elects, calls, justifies, and keeps. Protestants insist that grace is not a substance the church dispenses so much as the Father's gift in the Son, applied by the Spirit through the Word.

Churches differ on whether grace can be resisted and whether it is particular to the elect. They agree that salvation is of the Lord and that boasting is excluded.
protestant.faith_and_works:
The Reformation confession is faith alone, sola fide: we are justified by faith apart from works of the law. That faith is never alone; it works through love. Works are the fruit and evidence of a living trust, not the currency with which acceptance is purchased.

James and Paul are read together: a faith that produces no obedience is dead, yet the obedience does not justify. Protestant pastoral speech therefore presses both assurance in Christ and a life that matches the gospel.
protestant.predestination:
Predestination is God's eternal purpose concerning salvation. Protestants take the word from Scripture and then divide over its scope. Reformed churches teach unconditional election in Christ. Others teach that God predestines those he foreknows will believe, or they emphasize human response under prevenient grace.

All historic Protestant bodies deny that God is the author of sin. The doctrine is meant to humble pride and to ground comfort in God's mercy, not to invite despair or curiosity about the hidden will.
protestant.election:
Election is God's choosing a people in Christ. For some Protestants the elect are those God set his love upon before the foundation of the world; for others election tracks foreseen faith or the church as a body rather than a fixed list of names.

The pastoral use is the same across much of the family: Christians are to make their calling and election sure by trusting Christ and walking in his ways, not by seeking a private revelation of the decree.
protestant.repentance:
Repentance is turning from sin to God, with sorrow for sin and a purpose of new obedience. It belongs with faith at conversion and remains the daily habit of the Christian life. Protestants do not treat it as a sacrament administered by a priest, though confession to God and, when needed, to one another is urged.

Repentance does not earn pardon; it is the way pardon is received. Cheap grace that never turns is not the gospel they intend to preach.
protestant.means_of_grace:
Means of grace are the ordinary channels God uses to create and strengthen faith: the Word preached and read, the sacraments or ordinances, and prayer. Lutheran and Reformed churches use the phrase most readily; others speak of the same things as the church's appointed worship.

The means do not work as magic. They are effective because God has promised to meet his people there. Neglect of Word and Table is therefore treated as spiritually dangerous, not as a mere change of style.
protestant.original_sin:
Original sin is the fallen condition inherited from Adam: guilt and corruption that mark every human being from birth, apart from Christ. Protestants read Romans 5 and Psalm 51 as teaching a real fall, not only bad examples.

How infants are held in Adam, and how baptism relates to that guilt, is not agreed across Lutheran, Reformed, and Baptist churches. The shared confession is that no one enters the kingdom by native goodness.
protestant.human_nature:
Human nature after the fall is a fallen nature: still the image of God, still capable of civic virtue and of hearing the Word, yet bent toward self and unable to raise itself to saving faith without grace. Protestants resist both the claim that the fall only nicked us and the claim that we have ceased to be human.

Christ took this nature, without sin, to redeem it. The Christian hope is not escape from humanity but its healing.
protestant.image_of_god:
The image of God, the imago Dei, is what marks humankind as created for fellowship with God and for responsible rule over the earth. The fall defaced the image; it did not erase it. In Christ the image is renewed in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness.

Protestant ethics of personhood, justice, and the sanctity of life ordinarily begin here. The image is not reserved for the baptized or for one sex.
protestant.free_will:
Free will is one of the most divided Protestant topics. Some teach that after the fall the will is bound in spiritual things and is freed only by regenerating grace. Others teach a real power to accept or refuse the gospel, often by a prior assisting grace.

No mainstream Protestant body teaches that the will is a second savior. The argument is about how grace restores willing, not about whether God must save and whether humans are accountable.
protestant.mortal_and_venial_sin:
Protestants do not officially divide sins into mortal and venial as a sacramental system. They speak of sin and of willful sin, and they know that some acts destroy faith's profession while others wound a living faith. All sin is serious before God; not every failing proves a person was never converted.

Church discipline and pastoral care still distinguish stubborn, public rebellion from ordinary struggle. The remedy in either case is repentance and the blood of Christ, not a tally of weights.
protestant.total_depravity:
Many Protestants, especially in the Reformed stream, speak of fallenness or inability: every faculty is touched by sin, so that no one seeks God savingly by nature. Total depravity in that sense does not mean every person is as vicious as possible; it means there is no untouched corner that can take the first step to God.

Other Protestants state the same wound more mildly. Across the family the practical claim is that salvation must begin with God.
protestant.scripture:
The Bible is Scripture, the Word of God written, the church's final written authority for faith and life. Protestants put the canonical books in the hand of the people and in the pulpit. Preaching is exposition of this book, not a substitute for it.

Translations are many; the conviction is one: God has spoken in these writings so that the church may be taught, reproved, and equipped.
protestant.canon:
The Protestant canon is commonly the sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments. The books the Western church called deuterocanonical are read by some for edification and omitted from the rule of faith by most.

The canon is received as the apostolic witness, closed with the death of the apostles. Adding later scriptures as equal to these books is rejected.
protestant.sola_scriptura:
Sola scriptura, Scripture alone, means that Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and practice. Creeds, councils, and teachers are valuable and are not discarded; they stand under the text and may be corrected by it.

The slogan is not 'no tradition' and not 'private whim.' It is the claim that when church and Bible appear to clash, the church must yield.
protestant.inspiration:
Inspiration is God's having breathed out the words of Scripture through human writers, so that what they wrote is God's Word. Protestants speak of verbal inspiration to insist that the wording, not only the general ideas, is of God, while still acknowledging the writers' styles and circumstances.

The doctrine supports confidence in preaching and translation. It is not a theory of dictation that erases the human voice of Moses or Paul.
protestant.inerrancy:
Many Protestants speak of the infallibility of Scripture: it will not lead the church astray in what God intends to teach. In the last two centuries a stricter word, inerrancy, has been used in parts of the family for freedom from error in all the Bible affirms.

Other Protestants prefer to speak of the Bible's truthfulness in matters of salvation and faith without extending the claim to every historical or scientific detail. The debate is internal; both sides mean to honor the book as God's Word.
protestant.apocrypha:
Protestants typically call the extra Old Testament books the Apocrypha or deuterocanonical books. Anglican and some Lutheran lectionaries still read them. Most other churches leave them outside public reading and doctrine.

They are not treated as empty of wisdom. They are treated as falling short of the authority of the Law, the Prophets, and the apostolic writings.
protestant.open_canon:
Protestants confess a closed canon. The church may translate, preach, and apply the Bible; it may not place later revelations, new scriptures, or a living prophet on the same shelf as Isaiah and Paul.

Private guidance and congregational discernment are not denied. They are tested by the closed book.
protestant.continuing_revelation:
The sufficiency of Scripture, sometimes called closed revelation in this sense, means public revelation for the whole church ended with the apostolic witness. God still illumines readers and may guide by providence and by gifts, but he does not add chapters to the Bible.

Movements that claim new binding scripture or a restored office of revealing apostle stand outside this Protestant rule, even when they use Protestant language in other respects.
protestant.hermeneutics:
Hermeneutics is the disciplined reading of Scripture. Protestants encourage private interpretation in the sense that every believer may and should read. They do not mean that every reading is equal. The analogy of Scripture, the plain sense, the original languages, and the gathered church's confession all restrain isolated novelty.

The Reformation put the book in the vernacular so that interpretation would be common, not clerical only.
protestant.tradition:
Tradition is the church's handed-on teaching and practice. Protestants honor it when it agrees with Scripture and correct it when it does not. The early creeds and the Reformation confessions are tradition of that sort: servants of the text, not rivals to it.

Unwritten traditions that bind the conscience without biblical warrant are refused. Custom in worship may be kept for order and charity.
protestant.magisterium:
Protestants do not name a Magisterium in the Roman sense. Teaching authority belongs to Scripture as it is opened in preaching, confession, and mutual correction. No single see is the court of last appeal.

Confessional churches still expect members and ministers to teach in agreement with their standards, subject to the Bible.
protestant.papal_primacy:
Protestants regard the papacy as a historically developed office of the bishop of Rome, not as a primacy instituted by Christ over the whole church. They may speak respectfully of particular popes; they do not accept universal jurisdiction as a mark of the true church.

The keys, in Protestant reading, belong to the preaching of the gospel and to discipline in the local and regional church.
protestant.papal_infallibility:
Papal infallibility is rejected. No bishop, including the bishop of Rome, is preserved from error when defining doctrine. The church as a whole may err and has erred; Scripture remains the test.

This refusal is one of the oldest Protestant disagreements with Rome and is not limited to one party within Protestantism.
protestant.ecumenical_councils:
Protestants receive the early councils, especially Nicaea and Chalcedon, as faithful witnesses to Scripture on the Trinity and the person of Christ. They do not bind themselves to every later council of the medieval West.

A council is authoritative insofar as it agrees with the apostles' writing. The number of councils is therefore not itself an article of faith.
protestant.apostolic_succession:
Apostolic succession, for most Protestants, is succession in apostolic doctrine more than an unbroken chain of hand-laying. Some Anglican and Lutheran churches also value historic episcopal succession as a sign of continuity, without making it the essence of the church.

A church that preaches the apostles' gospel and administers the Christ's signs is apostolic, even if its paperwork of bishops is thin.
protestant.priesthood_authority:
Ministerial authority is authority to preach the Word, administer the sacraments or ordinances, and shepherd, derived from Christ through the church's call, not a separate priestly caste that stands between God and the people.

The minister is a steward. The congregation retains the duty to judge teaching by Scripture.
protestant.church:
The church is the body of Christ, the company of those who belong to him by faith, gathered in visible congregations and stretching across time and place. Protestants speak of both the church they can see and the church God knows.

It is created by the Word, not by bloodline or by a single earthly head. To be in Christ is to be joined to his people.
protestant.one_true_church:
Protestants ordinarily locate the true church wherever the gospel is purely preached and the sacraments or ordinances are rightly administered, sometimes adding godly discipline. That true church is finally the company of the elect, known fully only to God, and is not identical with one denomination.

Visible churches may be more or less faithful. The claim that only one institution is the church is refused.
protestant.marks_of_the_church:
The marks of the church in Reformation speech are the Word and sacrament: the gospel preached and baptism and the Lord's Supper administered according to Christ's institution. Some add church discipline as a third mark.

These marks let Christians recognize a church without requiring a particular hierarchy or a particular name on the door.
protestant.visible_and_invisible_church:
The distinction between the invisible church and the visible church is classic Protestant language. The invisible church is all who are truly in Christ. The visible church is the mixed company of professing believers and their children, among whom hypocrites may also sit.

The distinction warns against despair when the visible church is stained, and against presumption that membership rolls equal election.
protestant.polity:
Church government, or polity, among Protestants is episcopal, presbyterian, or congregational, and sometimes a blend. No one form is agreed to be essential to the existence of the church, though each party will argue its form from Scripture.

Order is required; a particular chain of command is not the gospel.
protestant.local_church:
The local church is the congregation that meets around Word and Table in a place. It is a real church, not a branch office with no spiritual standing. Connection to other churches is valued in different degrees, from tight synods to loose fellowships.

Pastoral care, discipline, and the sacraments happen here.
protestant.church_discipline:
Church discipline is the church's duty to admonish, and if need be to exclude, a member who persists in serious sin or false teaching. Its aim is repentance and the purity of the Table, not humiliation.

Excommunication in Protestant practice is a solemn last step and is meant to be reversible upon repentance. Neglect of discipline is treated as unfaithfulness to the Lord's command.
protestant.ecumenism:
Christian unity, often called ecumenism, is the search for visible fellowship among churches that confess the same Lord. Protestants have built councils, unions, and partnerships, and they have also divided when they judged the gospel at stake.

Unity is not purchased by silencing Scripture. It is sought where the gospel is shared.
protestant.schism:
Schism is sinful division of the body. Protestants admit their history is full of splits, some for the gospel and some for pride or taste. They distinguish leaving error from tearing a church over indifferent things.

The remedy is repentance, patience, and a return to the marks of the church rather than nostalgia for a single medieval structure.
protestant.ordination:
Ordination is the church's public setting apart of men, and in many bodies also of women, to the ministry of Word and sacrament or ordinance. Hands are laid on with prayer. The act recognizes gifts and a call; it does not inject a different priesthood.

Some churches require a bishop's hands, others a presbytery or the local congregation. All treat an orderly call as normal.
protestant.priesthood:
The priesthood of all believers is the Protestant claim that every Christian has access to God through Christ and a share in the church's priestly service of prayer and witness. It does not abolish pastors. It abolishes a mediating caste.

Baptism, not ordination, is the basic consecration of the Christian.
protestant.episcopacy:
A bishop, or overseer, in some Protestant churches is a regional pastor of pastors. In others the New Testament bishop is simply the local elder. The word is kept or dropped according to polity.

Where bishops exist, they are not a third order necessary to the being of the church in the Roman or Eastern sense, except in parts of Anglicanism that argue otherwise.
protestant.elders:
Elders are the ordinary pastoral officers of many Protestant churches: men, and in some churches women, charged to teach, shepherd, and rule. Presbyterian churches distinguish teaching and ruling elders. Congregational churches may use pastor and deacon instead.

The office is local and collegial more often than monarchical.
protestant.deacons:
A deacon is an officer of service, charged with the church's mercy, finances, and practical care, after the pattern of Acts 6 and the Pastoral Epistles. In some churches deacons also share spiritual oversight; in others they do not.

The office is honored as ministry, not as a stepping stone only.
protestant.papacy:
The Pope is, for Protestants, the bishop of Rome, a prominent Christian leader whose claims of universal headship they do not accept. The papacy is a fact of history and of current world Christianity; it is not the necessary center of the church.

Criticism of particular papal acts is not the same as hatred of Catholic Christians.
protestant.priesthood_of_believers:
The priesthood of all believers means that every Christian may come boldly to the throne of grace and must bear the neighbor before God in prayer and the gospel before the neighbor in speech. There is one mediator, Christ.

The doctrine supports vernacular Bibles, congregational hymn singing, and the duty of ordinary members to test preaching.
protestant.clerical_celibacy:
Protestant clergy are ordinarily free to marry. Married clergy are treated as the New Testament pattern, not as a concession. Celibacy may be a personal gift; it is not a law of the office.

A minister's household is itself a field of discipleship and, when disorderly, a disqualification.
protestant.apostles_today:
Most Protestants hold that the apostolic age ended with the witnesses of the resurrection. There are no apostles today in that foundational sense. Missionaries and church planters may be called apostolic in a looser way.

New offices that claim equal authority with Peter or Paul to define doctrine are refused.
protestant.baptism:
Baptism is the washing with water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, commanded by Christ. Protestants agree that it is Christ's sign and seal, or ordinance, joining the baptized to the name of the Trinity and to the church.

They do not agree on infants, on whether it regenerates, or on dipping versus pouring. They agree it is not a human invention and is not to be repeated as if the first time were nothing.
protestant.mode_of_baptism:
The mode of baptism varies. Some churches immerse as the fullest picture of burial and rising with Christ. Others pour or sprinkle and regard the water and the name as the essence, not the quantity of water.

Disputes about mode have split congregations. They have not, in most Protestant theology, been treated as disputes about whether the other party is baptized at all, though some Baptist churches do so treat them.
protestant.confirmation:
Confirmation in Lutheran, Anglican, and some other Protestant churches is the baptized person's public confession of faith and the church's prayer for the Spirit's strengthening. It is not universally practiced and is not a third dominical sacrament in most Protestant counting.

Where it is kept, it belongs with catechesis. Where it is not, the same work is done in baptismal vows of adults and in reception into membership.
protestant.confession:
Confession of sins is made to God, and when injury has been done, to the neighbor. Some Lutheran and Anglican churches also provide private confession to a pastor with the word of forgiveness spoken in Christ's name.

There is no Protestant requirement to list every sin to a priest in order to be forgiven. There is a requirement not to hide from God.
protestant.anointing_of_the_sick:
Anointing the sick with oil and prayer, following James, is practiced in some Protestant churches as a request for healing and as a commendation of the sufferer to God. It is not a last rite that prepares the soul by its own power.

Healing is asked for; death is also prepared for. Either outcome is placed in the Lord's hands.
protestant.holy_orders:
What other churches call Holy Orders Protestants usually call ordination. It sets apart ministers; it does not confer a sacrificial priesthood that reiterates the Mass.

Anglican and some Lutheran speech still says Holy Orders. The function remains the ministry of Word and sacrament.
protestant.matrimony:
Christian marriage is a covenant between one man and one woman, in the classic Protestant confession, blessed by God and recognized by the church. It is not a sacrament in the Roman numbering for most Protestants, yet it is holy and not a mere civil contract.

The household is a school of discipleship. Churches now differ over divorce and over whether the classic definition may be revised; the inherited teaching is covenant faithfulness.
protestant.sacraments:
Protestants speak of sacraments or ordinances. The two they agree Christ instituted for all his people are baptism and the Lord's Supper. Some Lutheran and Anglican churches allow a broader honor to other rites without counting seven in the Roman manner.

A sacrament, in Reformation language, is a visible word joined to the promise of the gospel. It does not work apart from faith, yet it is more than a bare memorial in Lutheran and Reformed teaching.
protestant.real_presence:
How Christ is present at the Lord's Supper is a historic Protestant split. Lutherans confess a Real Presence in sacramental union with the bread and wine. Reformed churches speak of a spiritual presence received by faith. Baptists and many free churches teach a memorial or symbolic presence.

All refuse the idea that the church offers the body of Christ again as a propitiatory sacrifice. All insist the Supper is Christ's own meal.
protestant.eucharistic_sacrifice:
The Lord's Supper is a memorial of the sacrifice, a proclamation of the one death of Christ, not a repetition of it. Praise, thanksgiving, and self-offering rise from the table; Calvary is not extended as a new victim.

Lutheran language of a sacrifice of praise is thanksgiving, not a new atonement. This is one of the sharpest Protestant contrasts with the sacrifice of the Mass as they have understood it.
protestant.closed_communion:
Practice ranges from open communion, inviting all baptized believers who trust Christ, to closer tables limited to a denomination or a congregation. The question is how to guard the Table without denying that the church is larger than one party.

Almost all require that communicants be baptized Christians who examine themselves. The rest is house discipline.
protestant.temples:
Protestants do not build temples in the sense of houses for restricted rites of endowment. The body of the believer and the gathered church are the temple of the Holy Spirit. Church buildings are meeting houses for Word and sacrament, holy by use, not by inner rooms of graded access.

Pilgrimage to a particular stone house is not required.
protestant.liturgy:
A worship service, or order of worship, may be fully written or almost free. Lutheran, Anglican, and many Reformed churches keep a liturgy of Word and Table. Free churches order the same elements more loosely around preaching, prayer, and song.

Liturgy is meant to serve the gospel, not to replace it. Quaker meetings among the wider Protestant family may wait in silence; most other Protestants fill the hour with Scripture made audible.
protestant.prayer:
Prayer is speaking to the Father through the Son in the Spirit: praise, confession, thanks, and petition. It may be written or free, public or private. Protestants encourage the Lord's Prayer and the psalms as schools of prayer.

Prayer is not a technique. It is the child asking the Father who already knows.
protestant.liturgical_calendar:
Many Protestant churches keep a church calendar: Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, Pentecost. Others keep only the Lord's Day and perhaps Christmas and Easter, wary of binding the conscience to feast days.

The year is a servant of the gospel story. It is not a second law.
protestant.sabbath:
Protestants commonly treat Sunday as the Lord's Day, sometimes called the Christian Sabbath: a day of worship and rest in honor of the resurrection. How strictly work and recreation are limited varies from sabbatarian Reformed practice to a lighter festival Sunday.

Seventh-day observance exists on the Protestant margin. The main body does not treat Saturday rest as binding on the church.
protestant.sunday_worship:
Sunday worship, the Lord's Day assembly, is the ordinary weekly gathering for Word, prayer, song, and often the Table. Attendance is a serious duty of membership, though Protestant churches rarely police it as a canonical crime.

The day commemorates the rising of Christ. That, not imperial law, is the usual reason given.
protestant.icons:
Protestant attitudes to images range from Lutheran and Anglican church art to Reformed suspicion of images in worship. The fear is idolatry: teaching the faith by pictures in such a way that the heart rests on what the hand has made.

Pictures for teaching and memory are widely allowed. Bowing to them in worship is widely refused.
protestant.veneration:
What other churches call veneration of saints Protestants have often named the worship of saints and rejected. Honor for the faithful dead as examples is common; asking them to hear prayer is not the Protestant norm.

The distinction between veneration and worship is not trusted as a safeguard. Prayer is directed to God through Christ.
protestant.fasting:
Fasting is a biblical discipline of self-denial joined to prayer. Protestants commend it as voluntary, not as a law of days that merits grace. Some churches keep Lent; others fast as need and conscience dictate.

The point is to humble the flesh and to seek God, not to display holiness.
protestant.sacred_music:
Hymns and worship music carry the Word in song. Protestantism has been a singing movement: psalms, chorales, Watts and Wesley, and later gospel and contemporary songs.

Taste divides congregations. The test offered is whether the words are true and the people can sing them.
protestant.instrumental_music:
Most Protestant churches use instruments in worship. A minority, especially some Churches of Christ and some Reformed psalm-singers, refuse them as lacking New Testament command.

Where instruments are used they are servants of the people's song, not a concert in front of a silent church.
protestant.preaching:
Preaching, the sermon, is the central act of most Protestant worship: the Word of God opened and applied. The preacher is a herald, not a performer. The church is a hearing church.

A sacrament without the Word is not the Reformation pattern. A service of songs without a preached text is treated as thin.
protestant.mary:
Mary is the mother of Jesus, blessed among women, a model of faith who believed the promise. Protestants read her Magnificat and honor her as the virgin mother of the Lord.

They do not ordinarily build a separate system of Marian mediation. She points to her Son; devotion that rivals his uniqueness is refused.
protestant.theotokos:
Some Protestants, especially Lutherans and Anglicans, will say Mother of God or use Theotokos to mean that the one she bore is God in the flesh. Others prefer mother of Jesus to avoid later Marian piety.

The shared concern is Christology: she is mother of the person who is God and man, not mother of the divine nature as such.
protestant.immaculate_conception:
The Immaculate Conception as a required dogma is refused. Protestants hold that Mary was a sinner saved by grace, however uniquely chosen. Her blessedness is election and faith, not a separate preservation from original sin defined as dogma.

The silence of Scripture on the point is treated as decisive against making it binding.
protestant.assumption:
The Assumption as a defined dogma is not a Protestant article. Some hope that Mary was honored at death in a unique way; most leave her death with the rest of the saints who sleep in Christ.

What must be believed about Mary is what the Gospels require. The rest is not a test of faith.
protestant.perpetual_virginity:
Protestants divide on the brothers of Jesus. Many take the New Testament references as ordinary brothers and reject perpetual virginity. Luther and some early Reformers still held that she remained a virgin; that view survives in parts of Lutheranism and Anglicanism.

The point is not required for the gospel. It is debated as a reading of a few verses.
protestant.intercession_of_saints:
Prayer to saints is refused as lacking scriptural command and as crowding the one mediation of Christ. The communion of saints means the fellowship of the living and the dead in Christ, not a traffic of petitions through heavenly patrons.

Saints are remembered and imitated. They are not addressed as hearers of prayer.
protestant.relics:
Relics may be historical curiosities; they are not means of grace. Protestant reform emptied many reliquaries because trust had settled on bone and cloth rather than on the Word.

Respect for the bodies of the dead is Christian. Pilgrimage to their fragments as sources of power is not the Protestant way.
protestant.prayers_for_the_dead:
Prayers for the dead are generally omitted from Protestant public worship. The dead in Christ are commended to God at the funeral; the church does not thereafter seek to alter their state by Masses or suffrages.

Some Anglicans keep a milder remembrance. The Reformation majority held that the dead are past the church's intercession and await the resurrection.
protestant.canonization_of_saints:
Saints, in ordinary Protestant speech, are all believers, the holy ones of the New Testament letters. The church may remember outstanding witnesses; it does not run a process that declares a soul in heaven and assigns a cult.

A calendar of commemorations in Lutheran and Anglican books is memory, not canonization in the Roman sense.
protestant.heaven:
Heaven is the presence of God, the place or state where the redeemed see the Lord and wait, with or without an intermediate body, for the resurrection. It is gift, not wage.

Protestant hope is personal and corporate: to be with Christ, and at last to inherit a renewed creation, not a vague immortality of the soul alone.
protestant.hell:
Hell is the just judgment of God on final unbelief, often described as eternal punishment. Some Protestants now teach conditional immortality instead. The tradition as a whole has spoken with severity of a real exclusion from the joy of God.

The doctrine is preached as warning and as the dark edge of the cross, where Christ bore wrath for those who believe.
protestant.purgatory:
Purgatory as a third place of satisfying temporal punishment is rejected. Christ's work is sufficient. The souls of the faithful pass to Christ; the lost pass to judgment.

Growth and purification belong to this life and to the resurrection, not to a penitential realm the church can shorten by offerings.
protestant.intermediate_state:
The intermediate state is life with the Lord for the believer between death and resurrection. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, in the common Protestant reading of Paul.

A minority teach soul sleep. The majority speak of conscious rest with Christ, still awaiting the body's rising.
protestant.soul_sleep:
Most Protestants teach a conscious intermediate state, not an unconscious dead. A smaller Protestant and Adventist-adjacent stream teaches that the dead sleep until the resurrection.

Funeral preaching in the mainline of the family addresses the departed as with Christ, and the mourners as those who will rise.
protestant.resurrection_of_the_dead:
The resurrection of the dead is the raising of the body at the last day, the righteous to life and the wicked to judgment. Protestant hope is not a permanent discarnate soul.

Christ's resurrection is the pattern and pledge. Creeds that omit the flesh are treated as less than Christian.
protestant.last_judgment:
The final judgment, sometimes pictured from Revelation as the great white throne, is Christ's public verdict on every life. Believers are judged as those already justified, their works disclosed as evidence; the unrepentant meet the justice they would not have forgiven.

The Judge is the crucified and risen one. Fear and hope both look to him.
protestant.investigative_judgment:
Investigative judgment as a distinct heavenly review beginning in the nineteenth century is not a Protestant article. Judgment in Protestant speech is the decision God has already made in the gospel and will publish at Christ's coming.

Assurance rests on Christ's finished work, not on the outcome of a later audit of the books of those who already believe.
protestant.second_coming:
The Second Coming, the return of Christ, is personal, visible, and still ahead. Protestants live between ascension and appearing. No date is known.

Hope of his coming trains watchfulness and mission. It is not an escape hatch from present obedience.
protestant.millennium:
The thousand years of Revelation 20 divide Protestants into premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial readings. The text is canonical; the timetable is not agreed.

All expect Christ to win. None is permitted, in classical confession, to make a millennial chart the test of the gospel.
protestant.rapture:
The rapture, being caught up to meet the Lord, is a Pauline promise. Whether it is a secret removal years before a tribulation, or the public meeting of the church with Christ at one appearing, is debated, especially in evangelical Protestantism.

The comfort of the text is that the living and the dead in Christ will be together with him. The schedule is secondary.
protestant.annihilation:
The majority historic Protestant view of the lost is eternal conscious torment. A growing minority teaches annihilation or conditional immortality: the wicked finally perish.

Both sides claim Scripture. Neither side treats the question as the article by which the church stands or falls, though each regards it as grave.
protestant.degrees_of_glory:
Protestants commonly speak of one heaven and of differing rewards, not of three kingdoms of glory as graded destinies. All who are in Christ see the same Lord.

Parables of greater and lesser responsibility are read as rewards within salvation, not as separate salvations.
protestant.spirit_world:
Protestant speech for the realm of the dead is usually Hades or Sheol, or simply 'with the Lord' and 'under judgment.' A populated spirit world of work, preaching, and second chances after death is not standard teaching.

The dead wait. The living preach to the living.
protestant.new_creation:
The Christian hope ends in the new heavens and new earth, creation healed, God dwelling with his people, death gone. Heaven is not the last word if heaven means escape from the world God made.

Resurrection and new creation belong together. The church prays 'your kingdom come' with that landscape in view.
protestant.marriage:
Christian marriage is a lifelong covenant meant to display Christ's faithfulness to the church. Protestant wedding services cite Genesis and Ephesians more than a sacramental canon.

Mutual duties of love and honor are preached to both spouses. The estate is good; it is not required of all.
protestant.divorce:
Divorce and remarriage are the most painfully unsettled Protestant ethic. Some churches allow divorce only for adultery or desertion and restrict remarriage. Others receive divorced persons more freely at the Table and in a second marriage after repentance.

No Protestant body treats vows as trivial. The argument is over which wounds the Lord named as ending a marriage.
protestant.contraception:
Birth control is left largely to Christian conscience in most Protestant churches. Some oppose particular methods; few bind members with a single ban on all artificial contraception.

Children are a blessing. Prudence in family size is not, for most Protestants, a sin in itself.
protestant.abortion:
Historic Protestant teaching treats abortion as the taking of an unborn human life and therefore as grave sin, with room in some bodies for tragic exceptions debated in law and pastoral care. The unborn child is not a mere part of the mother.

Churches differ in political strategy. They do not differ much in the claim that this life belongs to God.
protestant.sexual_ethics:
Sexual ethics in inherited Protestant teaching reserve sexual union for marriage between man and woman and call the church to chastity in singleness. Desire is not itself sin; ungoverned desire is.

Contemporary Protestantism is divided over same-sex marriage and related questions. The older confessions are unambiguous; many present denominations are not.
protestant.tithing:
Giving and stewardship are required; a strict tenth is urged in some churches and treated as a useful pattern in others. Grace, not a temple tax, is the motive.

The poor and the ministry of the Word are the first claimants on the church's purse.
protestant.alcohol:
Wine appears in Scripture as gift and as snare. Protestants range from moderation to total abstinence. Drunkenness is sin in every party.

The Lord's Supper itself has been a test case: wine in some cups, juice in others. Charity toward the weaker conscience is the Pauline rule invoked on both sides.
protestant.pacifism:
Just war and pacifism both live inside Protestantism. Magisterial churches usually allowed the magistrate the sword. Anabaptist and later peace churches refused killing.

A Christian may not hate the enemy. Whether a Christian may bear arms for the neighbor's defense is the disputed point.
protestant.church_and_state:
Church and state are distinct offices. Protestant history includes state churches and free churches. The modern majority, especially in Baptist and free-church lands, defends a limited state and a church that does not coerce faith.

The magistrate is under God. The church does not take the sword to make disciples.
protestant.oaths:
Most Protestants allow oaths in court when truth and neighbor require them, taking Jesus' words as a ban on casual swearing rather than on all solemn oaths. Quakers and some Anabaptists refuse oaths and offer affirmations instead.

Truth-telling is the substance. The form follows conscience and the law of the land.
protestant.food_laws:
All foods clean is the common Protestant reading of the New Testament. Mosaic food laws are not binding on the church. Thanksgiving, not a kitchen code, sanctifies the meal.

Wisdom about health and about food offered to idols remains. A second Leviticus for Gentiles does not.
protestant.ordination_of_women:
Women in ministry divide Protestantism. Some churches ordain women as pastors and bishops; others reserve the pulpit and eldership to men and encourage women's gifts in other offices. Both claim Scripture.

The dispute is about office, not about whether women are heirs of the kingdom or gifted by the Spirit.
protestant.headship:
Headship language from Paul is read by some as a permanent pattern of male leadership in home and church, and by others as a first-century frame that no longer restricts office. Roles of men and women are therefore one of the live Protestant arguments.

Marriage as mutual service is affirmed even where hierarchy is taught. Dignity is not the point in dispute; authority is.
protestant.head_covering:
Head covering in worship is a minority Protestant practice, kept in some conservative and Anabaptist congregations as obedience to 1 Corinthians 11. Most churches treat the passage as bound to its culture and do not require a veil.

Modesty and propriety in worship remain concerns even where the covering has fallen away.
protestant.mormon_label:
Mormon is the name Protestants have long used for Latter-day Saints. It is a label from outside that community's present preferred speech. In Protestant controversy it has often signaled a dispute over whether that community's additional scriptures and account of God fall within the historic church.

Fair speech uses the name a people give themselves while still stating the doctrinal disagreement.
protestant.roman_catholic_label:
Protestants say Roman Catholic or Catholic for the church in communion with the bishop of Rome. They do not concede that catholic, meaning the universal church, belongs only to that communion.

The adjective Roman marks the point of dispute: the papacy and the teachings attached to it, not the baptism or the confession of the Trinity shared with that church.
protestant.separated_brethren:
Other denominations are, in Protestant speech, other churches of Christ when they keep the gospel, and sects or errors when they do not. The language is uneven and often unkind in practice.

The intended claim is that the body of Christ is wider than one organization and narrower than every group that uses Jesus' name.
